hook: The San Francisco and San Mateo Railway's Geneva car barn and office building, built 1901; a San Francisco landmark since 1985.

historical_record.description: Built 1901 as the San Francisco and San Mateo Railway's company car house and office building at San Jose and Geneva avenues; by the 1920s it housed more streetcars than any other barn in the city's electric-car era.
Transferred to the Municipal Railway (MUNI) in 1944 along with the rest of the Market Street Railway system.
Designated a San Francisco landmark as the Geneva Office Building in 1985.
Severely damaged in the Loma Prieta earthquake, prompting MUNI to abandon the building for operations.
Transferred to the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department for use as an arts and history center, pending rehabilitation funding.

The San Francisco and San Mateo Electric Railroad broke ground for its Geneva Avenue Shops on 15 July 1900 and opened them on 22 April 1901; the power house was finished later that year. The brick complex held four buildings — a two-storey office with a single-storey transformer room attached, a twenty-track car shed and a blacksmith's shop. The office is 45 feet high and about 122 by 47 feet, wood-framed with unreinforced brick walls inside and out, in a late Romanesque Revival with Queen Anne corner turrets.
The design is generally attributed to the Reid Brothers — James W. and Merritt Reid — though a 1998 review of the record found neither original drawings nor a primary source naming them.

The building is one of the few in San Francisco still showing physical damage from the earthquake of 18 April 1906: the whole second-floor wall on the north elevation came down, and part of the matching section on the east. The repairs were wood-framed, with diagonal bracing added in the window arches, and the building was back in full use by 10 May 1906. By 1928 the rebuilt walls had been wrapped in tar paper, which is still there.

The office was the headquarters of a funeral car service that ran until March 1916 — three electric cars fitted with a coffin compartment at the front, a coffin elevator and seats for mourners behind, running on spurs off the electric road to cemeteries around the city.

After the carmen's strikes of 1906, 1907 and 1917 the United Railroads altered the office: the second floor was opened up as a social hall that could be converted into dormitories for live-in strike-breakers, and a door was cut into the east wall so they could reach the yard without meeting the strikers.

The power house was altered in 1910: its multi-paned windows were changed, the central bay's openings widened under shallow segmental arches, and the outer west and south walls encased in cement from the mezzanine up.

The city made the Geneva Office Building a landmark in 1986 — City Landmark No. 180. In 1995 FEMA found the office and the power house eligible for the National Register and the State Historic Preservation Officer agreed. A 1998 proposal by Muni to demolish both would have made it the first San Francisco landmark deliberately pulled down.

From 1956 to 1979 the Geneva Avenue yard was the only working streetcar depot in the Bay Area. The car barn beside the office was demolished in the late 1970s, the power house was abandoned before 1981 when a new grid was laid in for the Boeing light rail vehicles, and the office stayed in use until the Loma Prieta earthquake damaged and closed it in October 1989.
